He did not decide to keep them there. He simply never moved them, and by June it would have felt like a kind of violence to pick them up.

That was the summer the tractor threw its belt twice and the well pump started coughing air. He fixed what he could and let the rest go. The grass grew high between the rows. He mowed half the hillside in July and meant to finish the other half, but the heat came on hard, and the evenings were long and quiet, and he found himself sitting on the porch until dark with the radio off, listening to the trees.

Ruth had kept the books. He found them in the rolltop desk, three ledgers in her small slanting hand, and he learned things he had not known: which years they had lost money, which years they had nearly lost the farm. She had never told him how close it had been. He sat at the desk a long time with the last ledger open, running his thumb down a column of numbers that ended in March.

Mara called on Sundays. She asked if he was eating, and he said he was. She asked about the crop, and he said it looked good, which was true. She asked if he had thought any more about what they had talked about, and he said he was thinking about it, which was not."}
